\mathbf{A}_{12} \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{G} \sigma^2_a \\
\mathbf{GA}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{21} \sigma^2_a &
\mathbf{G} \sigma^2_a
\end{pmatrix} \\ \ \\ \
= 
\begin{pmatrix}
\left[ \mathbf{A}_{11} +
\mathbf{A}_{12} \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1} \left( \mathbf{G} - \mathbf{A}_{22} \right) \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{21} \right]  & 
\mathbf{A}_{12} \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{G} \\
\mathbf{GA}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{21}  &
\mathbf{G}
\end{pmatrix} \sigma^2_a \\ \ \\ \
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{H}_{11} &
\mathbf{H}_{12} \\
\mathbf{H}_{21}  &
\mathbf{H}_{22}
\end{pmatrix} \sigma^2_a
$$
Where:
$$
\mathbf{H}_{11} = 
\left[ \mathbf{A}_{11} +
\mathbf{A}_{12} \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1} \left( \mathbf{G} - \mathbf{A}_{22} \right) \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{21} \right] \\ \ \\ \
\mathbf{H}_{12} = \mathbf{A}_{12} \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{G} \\ \ \\ \
\mathbf{H}_{21} =  \mathbf{GA}_{22}^{-1}\mathbf{A}_{21} \\ \ \\ \
\mathbf{H}_{22} = \mathbf{G}
$$

Note that $\mathbf{H}_{21} = \mathbf{H}_{12}^\top$ (see Covariance between $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$), so $\mathbf{H}$ is symmetric. Then:
$$
\text{Var}\left[ \mathbf{a} \right] = \mathbf{H} \sigma^2_a
$$

Where $\mathbf{H}$ is the relationship matrix that combines pedigree and genomic relationships (Legarra et al., 2009), with the animals in the order of $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ord}}$.

## Definition of $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$

**Aguilar *et al.* (2010)**

The mixed model equations need $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$, not $\mathbf{H}$. Aguilar et al. (2010) showed that $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$ has a simple form:
$$
\mathbf{H}^{-1} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} +
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{0} \\
\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{G}^{-1} - \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Where $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ is the inverse of the full pedigree matrix (animals in the order of $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ord}}$), and $\mathbf{G}^{-1}$ is the inverse of the blended matrix, $\mathbf{G}_w^{-1}$ (`Gw_inv`). Only the block of the genotyped animals changes.

## Calculation of $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$

Three inverses are needed:

1. $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ (all animals, in the order of $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ord}}$).
2. $\mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}$ (the inverse of the block $\mathbf{A}_{22}$, not the 22 block of $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$).
3. $\mathbf{G}_w^{-1}$ (`Gw_inv`, see Blending $\mathbf{G}$).

$\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{A}_{22}$ are symmetric positive definite, so they are inverted with `chol2inv(chol())`. 

Then, $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ plus $\mathbf{G}_w^{-1} - \mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}$ in the block of the genotyped animals (`a2_ids`).
```{r}
A_inv <- chol2inv(chol(A_ord)) # A^-1.
A22_inv <- chol2inv(chol(A22)) # (A22)^-1.
dimnames(A_inv) <- dimnames(A_ord)
dimnames(A22_inv) <- dimnames(A22)

Hinv <- A_inv
Hinv[a2_ids, a2_ids] <- Hinv[a2_ids, a2_ids] + Gw_inv - A22_inv
dim(Hinv)
```

Note: $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ is obtained here by inverting the dense $\mathbf{A}$ (fine for `r nrow(A_ord)` animals). For large pedigrees, $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ is built directly from the pedigree (Henderson's rules), because it is sparse: here only `r round(100 * mean(abs(A_inv) > 1e-10), 2)`% of its elements are not zero.

Checks:

1. $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$ is symmetric, with the animals in the order of $\mathbf{A}_{\text{ord}}$.
2. Only the block of the genotyped animals differs from $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$.
3. $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$ is the inverse of $\mathbf{H}$. $\mathbf{H}$ is built from the full expression of $\text{Var}\left[\mathbf{a}\right]$ (with $\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{G}_w$), written compactly as $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{A} + \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{D} \\ \mathbf{I} \end{pmatrix}\left(\mathbf{G}_w - \mathbf{A}_{22}\right)\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{D} \\ \mathbf{I} \end{pmatrix}^\top$, with $\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{A}_{12}\mathbf{A}_{22}^{-1}$ (see Variance of $\mathbf{a}$). Multiplying out gives the four blocks $\mathbf{H}_{11}$, $\mathbf{H}_{12}$, $\mathbf{H}_{21}$ and $\mathbf{H}_{22} = \mathbf{G}_w$.
```{r}
stopifnot(isSymmetric(Hinv), identical(dimnames(Hinv), dimnames(A_ord)))
stopifnot(identical(rownames(Gw_inv), a2_ids), identical(rownames(A22_inv), a2_ids))
stopifnot(identical(Hinv[a1_ids, ], A_inv[a1_ids, ])) # Rows of non-genotyped animals unchanged.

DI <- rbind(A12 %*% A22_inv, diag(length(a2_ids))) # (D ; I), rows in the order of A_ord.
H <- A_ord + DI %*% (Gw - A22) %*% t(DI)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(H[a2_ids, a2_ids], Gw, check.attributes = FALSE))) # H22 = Gw.
err <- max(abs(Hinv %*% H - diag(nrow(H))))
err # H^-1 H = I (up to rounding).
stopifnot(err < 1e-8)
rm(DI)
```


# Mixed model equations

As mentioned at the beginning (see Working model), the model is:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{y}_1 \\
\mathbf{y}_2
\end{pmatrix} =
\mathbf{X}
\mathbf{b} +
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{W}_1 & \mathbf{0} \\
\mathbf{0} &  \mathbf{W}_2
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{a}_1 \\
\mathbf{a}_2
\end{pmatrix} +
\mathbf{e}
$$
Which, in compact matrix notation, is:
$$
\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{Xb} + \mathbf{Wa} + \mathbf{e}
$$

The assumptions are:
$$
\mathbf{a} \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \  \mathbf{H} \sigma^2_a\right) \\ \
\mathbf{H} \sigma^2_a = \mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times K} \\ \ \\ \
\mathbf{e} \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \ \mathbf{I} \sigma^2_e\right) \\ \
\mathbf{I} \sigma^2_e = \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} \\ \ \\ \
\text{Cov}\left[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{e}^\top\right] = \mathbf{0}
$$

Where $K$ is the number of animals in $\mathbf{a}$ (all animals in the pedigree) and $N$ the number of phenotypes.


Then, the mixed model equations (MME; Henderson, 1984) are:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X^\top} \mathbf{R}^{-1}  \mathbf{X} &
\mathbf{X^\top} \mathbf{R}^{-1}  \mathbf{W} \\
\mathbf{W^\top} \mathbf{R}^{-1}  \mathbf{X} &
\mathbf{W^\top} \mathbf{R}^{-1}  \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{H}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_a}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\mathbf{b}} \\
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X^\top} \mathbf{R}^{-1}  \mathbf{y} \\
\mathbf{W^\top} \mathbf{R}^{-1}  \mathbf{y}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Where $\mathbf{H}^{-1}\frac{1}{\sigma^2_a} = \left(\mathbf{H}\sigma^2_a\right)^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^{-1}$. And:
$$
\mathbf{R}^{-1} = \left(\mathbf{I}\sigma^2_e\right)^{-1} = 
\mathbf{I}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e} =
\mathbf{I} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}
$$

Then the equation becomes:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X^\top} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}  \mathbf{X} &
\mathbf{X^\top} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}  \mathbf{W} \\
\mathbf{W^\top} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}  \mathbf{X} &
\mathbf{W^\top} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}  \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{H}^{-1} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_a}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\mathbf{b}} \\
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X^\top} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}  \mathbf{y} \\
\mathbf{W^\top} \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}  \mathbf{y}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $\sigma^2_e$ cancels the residual variance in the denominators:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X^\top}  \mathbf{X} &
\mathbf{X^\top}  \mathbf{W} \\
\mathbf{W^\top}  \mathbf{X} &
\mathbf{W^\top}  \mathbf{W} + \mathbf{H}^{-1} \frac{\sigma^2_e}{\sigma^2_a}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\mathbf{b}} \\
\widehat{\mathbf{a}}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X^\top}  \mathbf{y} \\
\mathbf{W^\top}  \mathbf{y}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Where $\alpha = \frac{\sigma^2_e}{\sigma^2_a}$. With heritability $h^2 = \frac{\sigma^2_a}{\sigma^2_a + \sigma^2_e}$, $\alpha = \frac{1 - h^2}{h^2}$.

# Restricted Maximum Likelihood

The MME need $\alpha = \sigma^2_e / \sigma^2_a$. Then, the variance components $\boldsymbol{\theta} = \left(\sigma^2_a, \sigma^2_e\right)^\top$ must be estimated first. The standard method is restricted (or residual) maximum likelihood, REML (Patterson and Thompson, 1971).

## Why REML and not ML

Under the model, $\mathbf{y} \sim N\left(\mathbf{Xb}, \mathbf{V}\right)$, with:
$$
\mathbf{V} = \text{Var}\left[\mathbf{y}\right] = \text{Var}\left[\mathbf{Wa} + \mathbf{e}\right] = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top\sigma^2_a + \mathbf{I}\sigma^2_e
$$
Because $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{e}$ are independent. $\mathbf{W}$ ($N \times K$) has one 1 per row, in the column of the animal with the record. Then, $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top$ is the block of $\mathbf{H}$ for the phenotyped animals, in the order of $\mathbf{y}$.

Maximum likelihood (ML) maximizes the likelihood of $\mathbf{y}$ as if $\mathbf{b}$ were known. It ignores that $\mathbf{b}$ is estimated from the same data, so the variances are biased downwards. For example, in $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{Xb} + \mathbf{e}$, ML gives $\hat{\sigma}^2_e = \text{SSE}/N$ instead of $\text{SSE}/(N - p)$.

REML uses only the part of the data that is free of $\mathbf{b}$. Let $\mathbf{S}$ be any $N \times (N - p)$ matrix of full column rank with $\mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$ (for example, $N - p$ linearly independent columns of $\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{X}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$). Each element of $\mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{y}$ is a linear combination of the records in which the fixed effects cancel out (an error contrast):
$$
\mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{Xb} + \mathbf{S}^\top\left(\mathbf{Wa} + \mathbf{e}\right) = \mathbf{S}^\top\left(\mathbf{Wa} + \mathbf{e}\right) \sim N\left(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{V}\mathbf{S}\right)
$$
REML is ML applied to $\mathbf{S}^\top\mathbf{y}$ instead of $\mathbf{y}$. Its distribution does not depend on $\mathbf{b}$, and the $p$ degrees of freedom used by the fixed effects are accounted for ($N - p$ contrasts instead of $N$ records). The result does not depend on the choice of $\mathbf{S}$, and $\mathbf{S}$ is never computed: the REML log-likelihood below is written with $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ only.

## REML log-likelihood

$$
L(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = -\frac{1}{2}\left[
\log\left|\mathbf{V}\right| +
\log\left|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right| +
\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y}
\right] + \text{constant}
$$

Where $\mathbf{P}$ is the projection matrix:
$$
\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{V}^{-1} - \mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\left(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}
$$

$\mathbf{P}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$, so $\mathbf{P}$ removes the fixed effects, and $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{V}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right)$, where $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the generalized least squares solution ($\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{y}$). The three terms of $L$ are:

1. $\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} = \left(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right)^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right)$: a weighted sum of squares of residuals.
2. $\log\left|\mathbf{V}\right|$: depends only on the variance structure.
3. $\log\left|\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{V}^{-1}\mathbf{X}\right|$: a penalty for estimating $\mathbf{b}$. This is the term that ML does not have.

## Maximizing $L$

$L$ has no closed-form maximum, so $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is found iteratively from the derivatives of $L$. $\mathbf{V}$ is linear in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$, with:
$$
\mathbf{V}_a = \frac{\partial \mathbf{V}}{\partial \sigma^2_a} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top \\ \
\mathbf{V}_e = \frac{\partial \mathbf{V}}{\partial \sigma^2_e} = \mathbf{I}
$$

First derivatives (score), for $i \in \{a, e\}$:
$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_i} =
-\frac{1}{2}\left[
\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\right) -
\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y}
\right]
$$

At the maximum the score is zero: the quadratic form of the data, $\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y}$, equals its expected value, $\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\right)$.

Second derivatives. There are three versions of the information matrix ($2 \times 2$), with elements:

| Information | Element $(i, j)$ | Method |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Observed, $-\partial^2 L / \partial\theta_i\partial\theta_j$ | $\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_j\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_j\right)$ | Newton-Raphson |
| Expected (Fisher) | $\frac{1}{2}\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_j\right)$ | Fisher scoring |
| Average (AI) | $\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_j\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y}$ | AI-REML (Gilmour et al., 1995) |

The AI matrix is the average of the observed and the expected information. It has no trace terms, so it is cheap to compute. Each iteration updates $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ as:
$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t+1)} = \boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)} + \left(\mathbf{AI}^{(t)}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}}\bigg|_{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(t)}}
$$

At convergence, $\text{Var}\left[\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right] \approx \mathbf{AI}^{-1}$, which gives the standard errors of the estimates.

## Computing $L$ and its derivatives from the MME

When $N$ is large, $\mathbf{V}$ ($N \times N$) is too large to invert. Then, everything is obtained from the MME (see Mixed model equations), with $\mathbf{T} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{X} & \mathbf{W} \end{pmatrix}$ and the coefficient matrix:
$$
\mathbf{C} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} & \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{W} \\
\mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{X} & \mathbf{W}^\top\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{H}^{-1}\alpha
\end{pmatrix}
$$

The key identity is:
$$
\mathbf{P} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2_e}\left(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{T}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{T}^\top\right)
$$

With the MME solutions $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$, and the residuals $\hat{\mathbf{e}} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\hat{\mathbf{b}} - \mathbf{W}\hat{\mathbf{a}}$, it gives:
$$
\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2_e} \\ \
\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2_e}
$$

**Log-likelihood** (e.g., Meyer, 1989), where $p$ is the number of columns of $\mathbf{X}$ (full rank) and $\log\left|\mathbf{H}\right|$ goes into the constant:
$$
-2L = (N - p - K)\log\sigma^2_e + K\log\sigma^2_a + \log\left|\mathbf{C}\right| + \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2_e} + \text{constant}
$$

**Score.** $\mathbf{C}^{22}$ is the block of $\mathbf{C}^{-1}$ for $\mathbf{a}$, with $\text{Var}\left[\mathbf{a} - \hat{\mathbf{a}}\right] = \mathbf{C}^{22}\sigma^2_e$ (prediction error variance, PEV):
$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigma^2_a} =
\frac{1}{2}\left[
\frac{\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top\mathbf{H}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{a}}}{\sigma^4_a} -
\frac{K}{\sigma^2_a} +
\frac{\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{C}^{22}\right)\sigma^2_e}{\sigma^4_a}
\right] \\ \ \\ \
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \sigma^2_e} =
\frac{1}{2}\left[
\frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}^\top\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^4_e} -
\frac{N - p - K}{\sigma^2_e} -
\frac{\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{C}^{22}\right)}{\sigma^2_a}
\right]
$$

**AI matrix.** The vectors $\mathbf{V}_i\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y}$ are:
$$
\mathbf{V}_a\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} = \frac{\mathbf{W}\hat{\mathbf{a}}}{\sigma^2_a} \\ \
\mathbf{V}_e\mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{\sigma^2_e}
$$

With $\mathbf{F} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{W}\hat{\mathbf{a}}/\sigma^2_a & \hat{\mathbf{e}}/\sigma^2_e \end{pmatrix}$ ($N \times 2$), $\mathbf{AI} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{P}\mathbf{F}$, and by the key identity:
$$
\mathbf{AI} = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2_e}\left(\mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{F}^\top\mathbf{T}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\mathbf{T}^\top\mathbf{F}\right)
$$

That is, the MME are solved with the two columns of $\mathbf{F}$ in place of $\mathbf{y}$ (right-hand side $\mathbf{T}^\top\mathbf{F}$).

## EM-REML

Setting both scores to zero and rearranging gives (Mrode, 2014, Eqns 17.5 and 17.6):
$$
\sigma^2_e = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top\hat{\mathbf{e}}}{N - p} \\ \ \\ \
\sigma^2_a = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top\mathbf{H}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{a}} + \text{tr}\left(\mathbf{H}^{-1}\mathbf{C}^{22}\right)\sigma^2_e}{K}
$$

Used as an update (right-hand sides computed with the current $\boldsymbol{\theta}$), this is the EM algorithm (Dempster et al., 1977): $\sigma^2_e$ comes from the residuals, and $\sigma^2_a$ from the predicted breeding values plus their PEV. The estimates always stay positive, but convergence is slow. AI-REML converges in a few iterations, but an update can give a negative variance. Then, a common strategy is to start with a few EM iterations, or to use an EM step when the AI step goes out of the parameter space.

## AI-REML algorithm

1. Start values. For example, from a guess of heritability $h^2_0$ and the phenotypic variance $\sigma^2_y$: $\sigma^2_a = h^2_0\sigma^2_y$ and $\sigma^2_e = \left(1 - h^2_0\right)\sigma^2_y$.
2. Compute what $L$, the score and the AI matrix need: $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ (if $N$ is small), or the MME solutions $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}$ and $\mathbf{C}^{22}$, with $\alpha = \sigma^2_e / \sigma^2_a$ (if $N$ is large).
3. Compute $L$, the score and the AI matrix.
4. Update $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. A variance cannot be negative: if the update makes it negative, it is set to a small positive value (the boundary), and it stays there while its score is negative. An EM step is an alternative.
5. Repeat steps 2 to 4 until convergence (changes in $L$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ below a small tolerance, e.g., $10^{-6}$).
6. Report $\hat{\sigma}^2_a$ and $\hat{\sigma}^2_e$, their standard errors from $\mathbf{AI}^{-1}$, and the heritability $\hat{h}^2 = \hat{\sigma}^2_a / \left(\hat{\sigma}^2_a + \hat{\sigma}^2_e\right)$ (standard error by the delta method).

Note on Mrode (2014, Chapter 17): two formulas there seem to have misprints. $\mathbf{P}$ is printed without the first $\mathbf{V}^{-1}$ in the second term, and in Eqns 17.2 and 17.3 some signs and powers of the variances differ from the ones above. The expressions here are consistent with Eqns 17.5 and 17.6, and were checked numerically.

## AI-REML algorithm: implementation

**Which route.** Here there are $N$ = `r length(y)` records, but $K + p$ = `r K + ncol(X_ord)` equations in the MME. Factorizing $\mathbf{V}$ ($N \times N$) is much cheaper than factorizing $\mathbf{C}$, so $L$, the score and the AI matrix are computed directly with the formulas of Maximizing $L$: each line of code below is one formula. The MME route (Computing $L$ and its derivatives from the MME) gives the same numbers, and it is used below as a check. With many records (large $N$), the MME route, with sparse matrices, is the one to use.

### Data for REML

REML needs only $\mathbf{y}$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top$: $\mathbf{V}$ depends on $\mathbf{H}$ only through the phenotyped animals. $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{X}_{\text{ord}}$ are already aligned (see Align data with the ordered $\mathbf{A}$), and $\mathbf{H}$ was built in Calculation of $\mathbf{H}^{-1}$ (check 3).
```{r}
Hyy <- H[y_ids, y_ids] # W H W': block of H for the phenotyped animals, in the order of y.
stopifnot(identical(rownames(Hyy), names(y)), identical(rownames(X_ord), names(y)))
n_b <- ncol(X_ord)     # p in the formulas (`p` is already used for the allele frequencies).
c(N = length(y), p = n_b, K = K)
```

### Steps 2 and 3: $L$, score and AI matrix for a given $\boldsymbol{\theta}$

`reml_terms()` takes $\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\sigma^2_a, \sigma^2_e)$ and returns $L$, the score and the AI matrix. Two computational details:

- $\log\left|\mathbf{V}\right| = 2\sum_i \log u_{ii}$, where $\mathbf{U}$ is the Cholesky factor of $\mathbf{V}$ ($\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{U}$). The same factor gives $\mathbf{V}^{-1}$ (`chol2inv()`).
- $\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{V}_a\right) = \sum_{ij} p_{ij}\left(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top\right)_{ij}$, because both matrices are symmetric. This avoids the matrix product.
```{r}
reml_terms <- function(theta, y, X, Hyy) {
  sa <- theta[["sa"]] # sigma2_a
  se <- theta[["se"]] # sigma2_e
  N <- length(y)

  # V = W H W' sigma2_a + I sigma2_e, and V^-1 from its Cholesky factor (V = U'U).
  V <- sa * Hyy + se * diag(N)
  U <- chol(V)
  Vi <- chol2inv(U)

  # P = V^-1 - V^-1 X (X' V^-1 X)^-1 X' V^-1
  ViX <- Vi %*% X
  XViX <- crossprod(X, ViX)
  P <- Vi - ViX %*% solve(XViX, t(ViX))
  Py <- drop(P %*% y)

  # L = -1/2 [log|V| + log|X' V^-1 X| + y' P y]
  logL <- -0.5 * (2 * sum(log(diag(U))) + c(determinant(XViX)$modulus) + sum(y * Py))

  # V_i P y, with V_a = W H W' and V_e = I.
  VaPy <- drop(Hyy %*% Py)
  VePy <- Py

  # Score: dL/dtheta_i = -1/2 [tr(P V_i) - y' P V_i P y]
  score <- -0.5 * c(sa = sum(P * Hyy) - sum(Py * VaPy),
                    se = sum(diag(P)) - sum(Py * VePy))

  # AI_ij = 1/2 y' P V_i P V_j P y = 1/2 F' P F, with F = (V_a P y, V_e P y).
  Fm <- cbind(sa = VaPy, se = VePy)
  AI <- 0.5 * crossprod(Fm, P %*% Fm)

  list(logL = logL, score = score, AI = AI)
}
```

### Steps 1, 4 and 5: start values and iterations

`ai_reml()` runs the algorithm:

1. **Start values.** $\sigma^2_y$ is the residual variance of $\mathbf{y}$ after fitting only the fixed effects (ordinary least squares), and $h^2_0 = 0.3$.
4. **Update.** $\boldsymbol{\theta} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\theta} + \mathbf{AI}^{-1}\,\partial L / \partial\boldsymbol{\theta}$. A variance cannot be negative: if the update makes it $\le 0$, it is set to a small positive value, $\epsilon = 10^{-8}\sigma^2_y$ (the boundary). While a variance is at the boundary and its score is negative ($L$ would only increase if the variance were negative), it stays fixed, and only the other variance is updated, with its own element of $\mathbf{AI}$.
5. **Convergence.** Stop when the change in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (relative to $\sigma^2_y$) and the change in $L$ are both below $10^{-8}$.
```{r}
ai_reml <- function(y, X, Hyy, h2_0 = 0.3, tol = 1e-8, max_iter = 100) {
  # Step 1: start values.
  ols <- lm.fit(X, y)
  s2y <- sum(ols$residuals^2) / (length(y) - ncol(X))
  theta <- c(sa = h2_0 * s2y, se = (1 - h2_0) * s2y)
  eps <- 1e-8 * s2y # Boundary: smallest value allowed for a variance.

  history <- NULL
  logL_old <- -Inf
  converged <- FALSE
  for (iter in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    # Steps 2 and 3: L, score and AI matrix at the current theta.
    r <- reml_terms(theta, y, X, Hyy)
    history <- rbind(history, data.frame(iter = iter, sigma2_a = theta[["sa"]], sigma2_e = theta[["se"]],
                                         h2 = theta[["sa"]] / sum(theta), logL = r$logL))

    # Step 4: AI update. A variance at the boundary with a negative score stays fixed.
    free <- !(theta <= eps & r$score < 0)
    step <- c(sa = 0, se = 0)
    step[free] <- solve(r$AI[free, free, drop = FALSE], r$score[free])
    theta_new <- pmax(theta + step, eps)

    # Step 5: convergence.
    converged <- max(abs(theta_new - theta)) < tol * s2y && abs(r$logL - logL_old) < tol
    theta <- theta_new
    logL_old <- r$logL
    if (converged) break
  }

  list(theta = theta, converged = converged, history = history,
       at_boundary = theta <= eps, AI = reml_terms(theta, y, X, Hyy)$AI)
}
```

Run AI-REML on `delta`. Each row of the history is one iteration.
```{r}
reml <- ai_reml(y, X_ord, Hyy)
stopifnot(reml$converged)
reml$history
```

### Step 6: estimates and standard errors

At convergence, $\text{Var}\left[\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right] \approx \mathbf{AI}^{-1}$. The standard error of $\hat{h}^2 = \hat{\sigma}^2_a / (\hat{\sigma}^2_a + \hat{\sigma}^2_e)$ comes from the delta method: $\text{Var}\left[\hat{h}^2\right] \approx \mathbf{g}^\top\mathbf{AI}^{-1}\mathbf{g}$, with $\mathbf{g} = \partial h^2 / \partial\boldsymbol{\theta} = \left(\sigma^2_e, -\sigma^2_a\right)^\top / \left(\sigma^2_a + \sigma^2_e\right)^2$. If a variance is at the boundary, this large-sample theory does not apply: its standard error (and that of $\hat{h}^2$) is not reported (`NA`), and the other standard error uses only its own element of $\mathbf{AI}$.
```{r}
theta_hat <- reml$theta
free <- !reml$at_boundary
h2_hat <- theta_hat[["sa"]] / sum(theta_hat)

SE <- c(sa = NA, se = NA)
SE[free] <- sqrt(diag(solve(reml$AI[free, free, drop = FALSE])))
g_h2 <- c(theta_hat[["se"]], -theta_hat[["sa"]]) / sum(theta_hat)^2
SE_h2 <- if (all(free)) sqrt(drop(t(g_h2) %*% solve(reml$AI) %*% g_h2)) else NA

data.frame(parameter = c('sigma2_a', 'sigma2_e', 'h2'),
           estimate = c(theta_hat[["sa"]], theta_hat[["se"]], h2_hat),
           SE = c(SE[["sa"]], SE[["se"]], SE_h2),
           at_boundary = c(reml$at_boundary[["sa"]], reml$at_boundary[["se"]], reml$at_boundary[["sa"]]))
```

With the current data, $\sigma^2_a$ goes to the boundary: the REML estimate of $h^2$ for `delta` is 0. Then, $\hat{\sigma}^2_e$ is the residual variance of the model with only the fixed effects, as expected (with $\sigma^2_a = 0$, $\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}\sigma^2_e$). The profile log-likelihood shows it: for each $h^2$, $L$ is maximized over the total variance $\sigma^2_a + \sigma^2_e$, and $L$ decreases as $h^2$ increases.
```{r}
h2_grid <- c(0, 0.01, 0.05, seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1))
prof_logL <- sapply(h2_grid, function(h2) {
  logL_s2p <- function(s2p) reml_terms(c(sa = h2 * s2p, se = (1 - h2) * s2p), y, X_ord, Hyy)$logL
  optimize(logL_s2p, interval = c(0.1, 10) * var(y), maximum = TRUE)$objective
})
plot(h2_grid, prof_logL, type = 'b', pch = 19, xlab = expression(h^2),
     ylab = 'REML log-likelihood (profile)')
abline(v = h2_hat, lty = 2, col = 'red')
```

### Checks

**1. The MME route gives the same $L$ and score.** At the start values, $L$ and the score are computed again with the formulas of Computing $L$ and its derivatives from the MME (including $\log\left|\mathbf{H}\right|$, so that both $L$ are equal, not only up to a constant).
```{r}
theta_0 <- c(sa = reml$history$sigma2_a[1], se = reml$history$sigma2_e[1])
sa <- theta_0[["sa"]]
se <- theta_0[["se"]]

# W (N x K): one 1 per row, in the column of the animal with the record (order of A_ord).
W <- matrix(0, nrow = length(y), ncol = K, dimnames = list(names(y), rownames(A_ord)))
W[cbind(seq_along(y), match(names(y), rownames(A_ord)))] <- 1
Tm <- cbind(X_ord, W) # T = (X W)
stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), rownames(Hinv)))

# C = T'T + blockdiag(0, H^-1 alpha), and its inverse.
ia <- n_b + seq_len(K) # Rows and columns of a in C.
C_mme <- crossprod(Tm)
C_mme[ia, ia] <- C_mme[ia, ia] + Hinv * (se / sa)
U_C <- chol(C_mme)
C_inv <- chol2inv(U_C)

# MME solutions, residuals and C22.
sol <- drop(C_inv %*% crossprod(Tm, y))
a_hat <- sol[ia]
e_hat <- drop(y - Tm %*% sol)
tr_HiC22 <- sum(Hinv * C_inv[ia, ia]) # tr(H^-1 C22)
aHia <- sum(a_hat * (Hinv %*% a_hat))  # a' H^-1 a
logdet_H <- -c(determinant(Hinv)$modulus)

logL_mme <- -0.5 * ((length(y) - n_b - K) * log(se) + K * log(sa) + logdet_H +
                      2 * sum(log(diag(U_C))) + sum(y * e_hat) / se)
score_mme <- c(sa = 0.5 * (aHia / sa^2 - K / sa + tr_HiC22 * se / sa^2),
               se = 0.5 * (sum(e_hat^2) / se^2 - (length(y) - n_b - K) / se - tr_HiC22 / sa))

r_0 <- reml_terms(theta_0, y, X_ord, Hyy)
rbind(V_route = c(logL = r_0$logL, r_0$score), MME_route = c(logL = logL_mme, score_mme))
stopifnot(abs(r_0$logL - logL_mme) < 1e-6, max(abs(r_0$score - score_mme)) < 1e-6)
rm(W, Tm, C_mme, U_C, C_inv)
```

**2. A general-purpose optimizer finds the same maximum.** `optim()` maximizes $L$ directly (without derivatives), with $\sigma^2_a, \sigma^2_e \ge 0$.
```{r}
opt <- optim(par = theta_0, method = 'L-BFGS-B', lower = c(0, 1e-8),
             fn = function(t) -reml_terms(c(sa = t[[1]], se = t[[2]]), y, X_ord, Hyy)$logL)
rbind(AI_REML = c(theta_hat, logL = reml_terms(theta_hat, y, X_ord, Hyy)$logL),
      optim = c(opt$par, logL = -opt$value))
stopifnot(reml_terms(theta_hat, y, X_ord, Hyy)$logL >= -opt$value - 1e-6)
```

**3. The code recovers known variances.** Data are simulated with the same $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{H}$, with $\sigma^2_a = 6$ and $\sigma^2_e = 9$ ($h^2 = 0.4$), and AI-REML is run on each simulated data set. If $\mathbf{z} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, then $\mathbf{U}^\top\mathbf{z} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top)$, where $\mathbf{U}$ is the Cholesky factor of $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{H}\mathbf{W}^\top$. The fixed effects do not change the REML estimates, so all are set to 1. The mean of the estimates should be close to the true values (REML is not exactly unbiased in small samples).
```{r}
set.seed(2026)
theta_true <- c(sa = 6, se = 9)
U_H <- chol(Hyy)
sim <- t(replicate(100, {
  a_sim <- sqrt(theta_true[["sa"]]) * drop(crossprod(U_H, rnorm(length(y))))
  e_sim <- sqrt(theta_true[["se"]]) * rnorm(length(y))
  y_sim <- drop(X_ord %*% rep(1, n_b)) + a_sim + e_sim
  fit_sim <- ai_reml(y_sim, X_ord, Hyy)
  c(fit_sim$theta, h2 = fit_sim$theta[["sa"]] / sum(fit_sim$theta))
}))
rbind(true = c(theta_true, h2 = 0.4),
      mean = colMeans(sim),
      SE_of_mean = apply(sim, 2, sd) / sqrt(nrow(sim)))
```


# Conclusion.

We have few phenotypes. With this low ammount of data, it is impossible to get a reliable estimation of $h^2$. 

The estimated $h^2 \simeq 0$. We do not have enough information to estimate the variance component $\sigma^2_a$.

Subsequent estimations of additive values and propagation to SNP effect is just unreliable and missleading.
